claims.text: The rapidly solidified starting alloy is a homogeneous, supersaturated metastable solid solution.
The starting alloy contains finely dispersed nanometer-scale intermetallic clusters.
High-temperature exposure causes Ti/Zn-rich intermetallic compounds to coarsen and segregate.
Ti and Zn can form stable intermetallic compounds in Mg-rich multi-element alloys.
Ti/Zn-rich intermetallic phases can act as physical barriers to corrosion-front progression.
Intermetallic phases can serve as sites for localized electrochemical reactions in an Mg-containing alloy.
Larger and more unevenly distributed intermetallic particles create local electrochemical-potential differences.
The local potential differences caused by aged intermetallic particles facilitate micro-galvanic coupling.
Micro-galvanic coupling disrupts the uniformity of passivation films.
Thermal aging increases localized corrosion relative to the as-quenched condition.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit higher corrosion-current density and more pitting than the as-quenched control.
Intermetallic coarsening and segregation alter high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Thermally aged samples form thicker, compositionally altered, or less protective oxide scales than the as-quenched alloy.
Lightweight high-entropy alloys can be designed at densities near or below 6 g/cm3.
Differences among constituent properties naturally favor formation of stable intermetallic compounds during aging.

contradictions.description: The starting state is called a homogeneous metastable solid solution while also being described as containing pre-existing intermetallic clusters. A homogeneous single solid solution and a multiphase state containing clusters are not equivalent unless 'homogeneous' is explicitly limited to the matrix or to the spatial uniformity of the cluster dispersion.
